result.summary: Agamemnon, despairing, proposes flight, but Diomed and Nestor rally the council and Agamemnon offers Achilles vast gifts. Ulysses, Ajax and Phoenix go to Achilles, who refuses them, though he says he will decide at daybreak. They return with his answer and the Achaeans go to rest.

scenes.title: Council of despair
scenes.summary: Panic grips the Achaeans. Agamemnon proposes sailing home, Diomed refuses, and Nestor advises setting guards and holding a feast for counsel.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean army may be ruined by the Trojans camped near its ships.

scenes.title: Feast and Agamemnon's offer
scenes.summary: Sentinels are posted. At Agamemnon's feast Nestor urges reconciliation with Achilles, and Agamemnon lists great gifts. Envoys are chosen and set out.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon risks losing the war and his pride unless Achilles is won over.

scenes.title: Ulysses pleads; Achilles refuses
scenes.summary: The envoys find Achilles with his lyre and are fed. Ulysses repeats the offer, but Achilles rejects it, resolves to sail for Phthia and speaks of his two fates.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean fleet is in danger of burning; Achilles has to choose between a long life and undying fame.

scenes.title: Phoenix's own story and appeal
scenes.summary: Phoenix tells how he fled his father's curse and came to Peleus, and how he raised Achilles. He urges him to yield, citing the Prayers.
scenes.stakes: Phoenix fears the burning of the ships and losing the son he raised.

scenes.title: The tale of Meleager
scenes.summary: Phoenix tells how Meleager withdrew in anger during the Calydonian war and yielded too late to gain the promised rewards.
scenes.stakes: Calydon faces destruction, and Meleager loses his rewards by yielding late.

scenes.title: Achilles stands firm
scenes.summary: Achilles will not move and Ajax urges departure. Achilles says he will fight only if Hector reaches his ships. The envoys leave and Phoenix sleeps there.
scenes.stakes: Achilles holds his honour at the cost of the Achaean fleet.

scenes.title: Report to Agamemnon
scenes.summary: Ulysses reports Achilles' refusal. Diomed advises rest and a fresh battle at dawn, and all go to sleep.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans face the Trojan assault without Achilles.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles states his choice between long life and undying glory.
Phoenix's allegory of Prayers as the lame daughters of Jove.
Achilles says life, once gone, cannot be bought or harried back.

analysis.text: Honour and anger drive the book. Achilles weighs a lifetime of unrewarded service against Agamemnon's gifts and refuses to be bought.
The embassy shows the heroic gift-exchange culture, where honour is measured in tangible prizes and compensation can settle offences.

legacy.text: Phoenix's allegory of the Prayers, and Achilles' choice of a short glorious life, became classic images in Greek and later literature.

fun_facts.text: Achilles' remark about Egyptian Thebes and its hundred gates is one of Homer's earliest references to Egypt.

language_notes.text: Panic and Rout are personified as war spirits who accompany armies; Rout is the flight of a beaten army.
"Man by man" means individually, summoned quietly rather than by a public shout, so the enemy would not learn of the despair.
"Held their peace" means kept silent.
Refers to Agamemnon's earlier insult to Diomed's courage, in Book 4 when he reviewed the troops.
"Endowed you by halves" means Jove gave only one of two gifts, rank but not courage.
Mycene is Mycenae, Agamemnon's kingdom; the ships are the contingent he led from there.
"Foments" means stirs up or incites; a "clanless, hearthless outlaw" has no kin or home, a man outside all society.
"Behests of night" means the commands of nightfall: time to stop and eat.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted; "behooves" means is fitting or necessary for you.
"Is in himself a host" means a man favored by the gods is worth a whole army.
A tripod is a three-legged cauldron or stand; a talent is a measured weight of gold, a unit of wealth.
"Erewhile" means a short time ago; "went up into her couch" is a formal oath that he never slept with her.
"Comfortable ordinances" means agreeable, welcome commands; the people will obey his rule willingly.
"Instant with them" means urgently pressing them to persuade Achilles.
"Earth-encircling Neptune" is an epithet for the sea god, whose waters were thought to surround the land. Neptune is the Greek Poseidon.
"Cross-bar" is the yoke joining the two arms of the lyre, to which the strings were fastened.
Mixing "less water with the wine" means a stronger drink. Greeks normally diluted wine, so this signals warm welcome for honoured guests.
"We have had no scant of good cheer" means there has been no shortage of hospitality.
"Minerva and Juno" are the Greek Athena and Hera, both goddesses who favour the Achaeans.
"Erewhile" means "a short time ago." The oath claims Agamemnon never slept with Briseis, so she returns untouched.
"Cajoling" means persuading by flattery or coaxing; Achilles rejects Ulysses' smooth appeals.
"Gates of hell" translates the gates of Hades, the Greek underworld, which Achilles takes as an object of hatred.
"Meeds of honour" means prizes or rewards given as marks of esteem.
"Fruitling of my spear" means a captive won in war. Achilles refers to Briseis, whom Agamemnon took.
The Scaean gates were the main gates of Troy. The oak tree was a landmark on the plain near them.
"One prize" refers to Briseis, the woman Agamemnon took from Achilles.
"Cozen" means to cheat or deceive.
Orchomenus and Egyptian Thebes were proverbially rich cities. Thebes is said to have a hundred gates.
Pytho is Delphi, where Apollo's temple held great treasure offered by worshippers.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; here, if a god were to be kind enough to take away his years.
"Enamoured" means in love with; the concubine was a secondary woman living in the household.
The Erinyes (Furies) were avenging spirits who punished crimes against family, especially wrongs between parents and children; Amyntor invokes them to enforce his curse.
"Sit upon knees" means that Phoenix would never have a son to place on his knees, that is, he would remain childless. Jove of the world below is Hades.
"Broach" means to open a jar to draw off wine.
Phoenix personifies Prayers (Litai) as lame daughters of Jove who trail behind Sin (Ate); the allegory warns that refusing prayers brings ruin.
He alludes to traditional tales of heroes, such as Meleager, who were persuaded by gifts; Phoenix goes on to tell the Meleager story.
The Curetes and Aetolians were neighbouring peoples; the war over Calydon, a city in Aetolia, is told as a precedent for Achilles' own situation.
Hecatombs were large public sacrifices, originally of a hundred oxen; here simply lavish offerings to the gods.
Marpessa was carried off by Apollo; her husband Ides fought him for her. Her name Alcyone echoes 'halcyon', the kingfisher whose cry sounds mournful.
Althaea's brothers were killed by Meleager in the quarrel over the boar's spoils, hence her curse; the text only hints at this as 'her brother's death'.
Erinys is a Fury, an avenging spirit who carries out curses; Erebus is the dark region of the underworld.
A plough-gate was a measure of land, roughly what a plough team could work; the offer is a large estate.
"Be king as much as I am" means: share my status as an equal, rather than serving Agamemnon; Achilles invites Phoenix to side with him.
"Vain" here means futile: the embassy has accomplished nothing.
Ajax refers to the custom of blood-price: a killer could pay compensation to the victim's family and stay in the community.
"Fain" means gladly or willingly; "would fain be held" means wish to be regarded.
"Contumely" means insolent, humiliating abuse.
"Made their drink-offerings" means they poured wine to the gods, a customary act on leaving a host's table.
Lesbos was an island Achilles raided; Diomede was a captive woman taken there, as Iphis was from Scyros.
"Pledged them in cups of gold" means they welcomed the envoys by raising cups and drinking to them.
"Ilius" is Ilium, another name for Troy; "the goal of Ilius" means the successful end of the war there.
"Laid his hand over the city" means Jove (the Greek Zeus) is shielding Troy with his power.
"Sued" means begged or petitioned; Diomed says Agamemnon should not have pleaded with Achilles.
"Rosy-fingered morn" is the standard Homeric phrase for dawn, repeated throughout the poem.

context_notes.text: The Trojans' watch-fires on the plain were described at the end of Book 8, so this closes that scene.
Thrace, north of the Aegean, was proverbial for stormy winds.
Diomed, son of Tydeus, is the youngest of the leading Achaean warriors and a fierce fighter.
Sthenelus is Diomed's friend and charioteer. Ilius is Troy.
The trench and wall were built to protect the Achaean ships, so sentinels camp outside the wall.
Agamemnon took Briseis, Achilles' war prize, after being forced to give up his own prize; this quarrel caused Achilles to withdraw from the fighting.
Lesbos is an island that Achilles had raided; the women were part of the spoils.
Orestes is Agamemnon's young son, later famous for avenging his father's murder.
Hades is god of the dead, hated because death is final and cannot be moved by prayer or sacrifice.
Eetion was king of Thebe and father of Andromache, Hector's wife. Achilles sacked his city earlier in the war and took the lyre as plunder.
Ulysses and Ajax are envoys from Agamemnon, with Phoenix, Achilles' old tutor, who goes with them.
A talent was a measure of weight in gold. Tripods and cauldrons were prized bronze vessels, valued as wealth and gifts.
Briseis, daughter of Briseus, was Achilles' war prize. Agamemnon seized her, which caused Achilles' wrath and his withdrawal from the fighting.
Orestes is Agamemnon's young son, who later avenges his father's murder in other Greek tradition.
The war began when Paris took Helen, wife of Menelaus, Agamemnon's brother, to Troy.
Neptune is the sea god. Phthia is Achilles' homeland in Thessaly, ruled by his father Peleus.
Agamemnon had offered Achilles one of his daughters in marriage as part of his compensation.
Thetis is a sea goddess and Achilles' mother. She foretold his choice between a short glorious life and a long obscure one.
Peleus is Achilles' father, king of Phthia. Phoenix was sent as tutor and guardian when Achilles joined the expedition against Troy.
The Dolopians were a people living on the border of Phthia in Thessaly, and Peleus made Phoenix their ruler.
Agamemnon's embassy offers gifts to compensate Achilles; the chosen envoys, Phoenix, Ajax and Ulysses, are his friends and respected comrades.
Phoenix, Achilles' old tutor, is pleading with him to accept Agamemnon's gifts and return to battle, using this myth as an example.
Diana (Greek Artemis) was goddess of hunting; neglecting her first-fruits offering was a serious insult that demanded divine vengeance.
Phoenix, Achilles' old tutor and guardian, has just pleaded with him to accept Agamemnon's gifts and return to the fighting.
Patroclus is Achilles' closest friend, and he attends to the household here; his later death drives the plot.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' soldiers, and their ships are at one end of the Greek camp.
Diomed is a young, outspoken Achaean leader and a fierce fighter. He had earlier spoken bluntly to Agamemnon in the council.
Drink-offerings (libations) of wine were poured to the gods before sleep, marking the close of the evening.

literary_notes.text: Sudden storm winds lashing the sea mirror the sudden turmoil in the Achaeans' hearts.
Agamemnon's tears are likened to a stream pouring down a cliff, showing a king overwhelmed by grief.
Agamemnon says Jove deceived him, though his own conduct and the quarrel with Achilles helped bring the defeat.
Diomed contrasts honour with valour to sharply rebuke the king.
Nestor's stark either/or hints at the night's decisive events, including the embassy to Achilles.
The short, blunt admissions reveal Agamemnon's abrupt humbling, though his later demand for obedience undercuts the apology.
Agamemnon compares Achilles' stubbornness to Hades, implying that refusing to yield is inhuman; the argument is also self-serving.
Nestor's anxious glances, especially toward Ulysses, show him as the careful elder who understands how difficult the mission will be.
Achilles sings of heroes' deeds instead of fighting, showing him as cultured, withdrawn and preoccupied with glory even in his anger.
Achilles calls them dearest of the Achaeans despite his anger, which hints that his refusal will be painful rather than simple.
Hector rages "like a maniac", making his confidence in Jove's favour seem reckless and doomed.
The long inventory of gifts shows Agamemnon's attempt to measure honour in wealth, which prepares for Achilles' rejection.
Achilles' blunt opening signals that Ulysses' persuasion will fail.
Achilles compares himself to a mother bird who feeds her young and goes hungry, showing his unrewarded sacrifice.
Calling Agamemnon a "hound" insults him as shameless; the word implies impudence.
Achilles piles up impossible amounts of wealth, such as sands of the sea, to show nothing could sway him.
Cattle can be won again but a life cannot, which contrasts replaceable wealth with irreplaceable life.
The two fates anticipate Achilles' early death at Troy and the lasting fame it will bring.
The narrator shows Phoenix's tearful fear for the ships, setting an emotional tone different from Ulysses' calculated speech.
The homely detail of the baby Achilles spitting up wine on Phoenix's shirt shows Phoenix's tenderness and gives his appeal emotional weight.
Prayers become lame, wrinkled daughters of Jove, and Sin runs ahead of them; the image shows that repentance comes slowly after wrongdoing.
The warning that rejected Prayers ask Jove to send Sin upon the proud foreshadows Achilles' later suffering and the death of Patroclus.
Meleager's wrath and withdrawal mirror Achilles' own, so the tale works as a mythological exemplum aimed at him.
Vivid physical details of Althaea kneeling, beating the earth and weeping make her curse emotionally intense and ominous.
The warning about burning ships anticipates the Trojans' attack on the Greek fleet later in the poem.
Ajax's blunt description paints Achilles as harsh and unbending, showing how the Greeks perceive his pride.
Achilles compares his treatment to that of a vile tramp, showing how deeply the insult to his honour stings.
Achilles' limit on his refusal, fighting only if Hector reaches his ships, hints that he will eventually return to battle.
The long silence shows the Achaeans' dismay, while Diomed's blunt rebuke shows his confidence and independence.
The compact saying that rest brings strength and stay gives Diomed's practical advice a proverb-like authority.
The fixed phrase "rosy-fingered" for dawn is a formulaic epithet that marks the turn from night to the next day's battle.
